This page follows U.S. O*NET-SOC 39-1013.00, First-Line Supervisors of Gambling Services Workers (the fixed index assigns this asset the corresponding Chinese title; the text follows the official occupational scope). First-line gambling area supervisory roles vary greatly: slots, table games, card and betting areas, VIP rooms, cages and counters, surveillance and compliance, and integrated venues with hotels, food service, and entertainment. Supervisors may lead one area for one shift or manage multiple areas and shifts. Before comparing roles or development paths, check education and experience requirements; jurisdictional gambling employee licensing and background checks; responsible gambling, anti-money-laundering and compliance training; shift arrangements, including overnight and holiday shifts; and whether bankroll, account, and personnel management are included.

Test your interest with a tabletop exercise: given a wholly fictional gambling area shift assignment covering venue type and size, numbers of open tables and machines, available staff and positions, shift bankrolls and table limits, one machine fault or payout dispute, one compliance incident involving suspected cheating or underage entry, and required shift reports and ledger checks, write pre-shift briefings and station assignments, patrol and oversight points, identification and reporting routes for cheating and compliance incidents, payout and machine fault response, and fund and account reconciliation. Mark decisions that must be made by venue management or the responsible compliance department.

Signals worth considering: willingness to work overnight and rotating shifts over the long term, maintain attention in noisy, busy settings, and manage crews and funds under compliance and internal rules. Signals requiring caution: difficulty accepting overnight and holiday shifts, inability to concentrate for long periods in noisy environments, or disagreement with responsible gambling and compliance requirements.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute a hiring decision, ability score, or compliance or legal conclusion.

First decide whether you are willing to make gambling floor management a long-term career: working overnight and rotating shifts in noisy settings; supervising crews and funds under internal rules and jurisdictional regulations; and taking management responsibility for compliance and customer experience. Test this through the tabletop exercise and seven-day tasks on this page.

The work of first-line supervisors of gambling services workers follows a cycle of pre-shift briefing and station assignment, floor patrol and operations oversight, compliance, safety and cheating identification, payouts and machine fault response, fund and account reconciliation, and scheduling, performance and policy management. Before shifts, they check open table and machine counts, available staff and positions, shift bankrolls and table limits, and complete briefings. They assign staff to games and stations, determine daily table openings and staffing schedules, ensure all stations and games are covered each shift, and move dealers among games. During operations, they circulate among tables and machines, observe compliance with internal rules and jurisdictional regulations, and ensure prompt, courteous service. They observe gamblers for marked cards, card switching, card counting, or other signs of cheating and notify security. They enforce safety rules and report or remove hazards and underage, intoxicated, disruptive, or cheating patrons. They attend to patrons showing possible compulsive gambling and assist when needed. They verify and pay jackpots, oversee timely payouts, exchange currency as needed, and record and issue betting receipts. They reset slot machines after payouts, handle minor faults such as coin jams and tilt conditions, document fault details, follow up repairs, or recommend servicing. They review operating expenses, budget estimates, betting accounts, and collection reports, and set and maintain game bankrolls and table limits. They assess employee performance, write evaluations, and handle interviews, hiring, training, and scheduling. They set policies on gambling types, odds, and credit, and plan and organize activities and services for hotel and casino guests. Emphases vary considerably: slot areas focus on machine availability, payouts and faults; table games on rules, funds and cheating identification; cages and counters on fund and account accuracy; surveillance and compliance on regulatory adherence and incident reporting; and integrated venues on services across business formats and event organization.

Gambling occupations are often confused. Distinguish them by responsibilities and outputs. This occupation is a first-line management role whose main outputs are crew patrol, shift organization, and compliance oversight in gambling areas. Gambling dealers directly deal cards and operate table games. Gambling cage workers and gambling change persons and booth cashiers handle chips, cash, and exchanges at counters. Gambling surveillance officers and investigators conduct surveillance and incident investigations. Gambling and sports book writers and runners register wagers and relay information. Gambling managers oversee overall gambling operations and business results, with a wider management scope. First-line supervisors of entertainment and recreation workers, except gambling services, manage nongambling entertainment and recreation crews. Security guards maintain premises safety and order.

entries.answer: This page follows U.S. O*NET-SOC 39-1013.00, First-Line Supervisors of Gambling Services Workers (the fixed index assigns this asset the corresponding Chinese title): directly supervising and coordinating workers in designated gambling areas. Duties include circulating among tables and machines, observing operations, and ensuring all stations and games are staffed each shift; supervising operations under internal rules and jurisdictional regulations and ensuring prompt, courteous service; observing gamblers for marked cards, card switching, card counting, or other signs of cheating and notifying security; processing and verifying financial transaction paperwork and responding to complaints; verifying and paying jackpots, overseeing timely payout, resetting slot machines after payouts, handling minor faults such as coin jams and tilt conditions, documenting faults and following up repairs or recommending servicing; explaining game rules, betting limits, and other internal rules; setting and maintaining game bankrolls and table limits; attending to patrons showing possible compulsive gambling and assisting when necessary; overseeing complimentary vouchers, rooms, discounts, and other benefits; enforcing safety rules and reporting or removing hazards and underage, intoxicated, disruptive, or cheating patrons; assessing employees and writing performance evaluations; monitoring stations and games and reallocating dealers; determining daily table openings and scheduling accordingly; reviewing operating expenses, budget estimates, betting accounts, and collection reports; setting policies on gambling types, odds, and credit; and interviewing, hiring, training, scheduling, and evaluating employees.
entries.question: What do first-line supervisors of gambling services workers mainly do?

entries.answer: Responsibilities and outputs differ. This occupation is a first-line management role whose main outputs are gambling area crew patrol, shift organization, and compliance oversight. Gambling dealers directly deal cards and operate table games. Gambling cage workers and gambling change persons and booth cashiers handle chips, cash, and exchanges at counters. Gambling surveillance officers and investigators conduct surveillance and incident investigations. Gambling and sports book writers and runners register wagers and relay information. Gambling managers oversee overall operations and business results, with a wider management scope. First-line supervisors of entertainment and recreation workers, except gambling services, manage nongambling crews. Security guards maintain premises safety and order.

entries.answer: A more accurate assessment is that tools will take over processes such as station and shift scheduling, machine status and fault records, organizing betting, account and reporting data, and drafting incident records, while primarily augmenting the occupation overall. ILO research from 2023 shows wide variation in task exposure across occupations, with a relatively low share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations. Technical feasibility does not mean organizational adoption has occurred. Floor patrol, compliance judgments, cheating identification, and customer and employee handling must remain with trained, authorized personnel. The conclusion is therefore that ways of working will change rather than the occupation being replaced as a whole.

entries.answer: The on-site supervisor bears responsibility for floor order and compliance implementation during the shift. Gambling licensing and compliance determinations, suspicious transaction and anti-money-laundering reporting, cheating and criminal investigations, machine and electrical repairs, and handling underage, intoxicated or disruptive patrons must follow procedures and be handled by appropriately authorized and qualified personnel, compliance departments, and regulators. Pre-shift briefings, funds, accounts, and incidents must be recorded under applicable rules, and customer, employee, and account information must follow minimum-necessary handling. Outputs from machine monitoring, scheduling, account, and record tools do not constitute compliance conclusions or cheating determinations. Matters beyond your authority should be reported to compliance or venue management. This page does not replace jurisdictional gambling regulations, licensing and background checks, responsible gambling and problem gambling assistance requirements, anti-money-laundering and customer due diligence requirements, venue rules and betting limits, or fund, accounting and safety management policies.

title.text: First-Line Supervisors of Gambling Services Workers

subject.name: First-Line Supervisors of Gambling Services Workers
subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate workers in designated gambling areas: circulate among tables and machines, observe operations, and ensure all stations and games are staffed each shift; supervise gambling operations under internal rules and jurisdictional regulations and ensure prompt, courteous service; observe gamblers for signs of cheating such as marked cards, card switching, or card counting and notify security; process and verify financial transaction paperwork; respond to and resolve complaints; verify and pay jackpots, reset slot machines after payouts, make minor repairs or adjustments, or recommend servicing; maintain knowledge of games and cheating methods; explain game rules, betting limits, and other internal rules; set and maintain game bankrolls and table limits; record machine fault details and follow up repairs; attend to patrons showing possible compulsive gambling and assist when necessary; oversee complimentary vouchers, rooms, discounts, and other benefits; enforce safety rules and report or remove hazards and underage, intoxicated, disruptive, or cheating patrons; assess employees and write performance evaluations; monitor stations and games and reassign dealers to ensure staffing; determine daily table openings and schedule accordingly; review operating expenses, budget estimates, betting accounts, and collection reports; set policies on gambling types, odds, and credit; interview and hire employees; and train, supervise, schedule, and evaluate staff.
